back: Tastes sour, has a pH below 7, and turns blue litmus red, e.g. vinegar or lemon juice.
A substance that neutralises an acid, e.g. metal oxides, hydroxides and carbonates.
A base that dissolves in water. It has a pH above 7, turns red litmus blue and feels soapy.
From 0 to 14 (at Year 9). Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.
A substance that changes colour depending on the pH, e.g. litmus, universal indicator or red cabbage juice.
Acids turn blue litmus red. Alkalis turn red litmus blue. Neutral solutions don't change either colour.
Red (strong acid) → orange → yellow → green (neutral) → blue → purple (strong alkali).
An acid and a base reacting to cancel each other out: acid + base → salt + water.
The compound made when an acid reacts with a base, e.g. sodium chloride or copper sulfate.

front: Which salts do hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acid make?
back: Hydrochloric → chlorides. Sulfuric → sulfates. Nitric → nitrates.
Salt + hydrogen, e.g. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen.
Salt + water + carbon dioxide, e.g. calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide.
Citric acid (citrus fruit), ethanoic acid (vinegar), hydrochloric acid (stomach), carbonic acid (fizzy drinks).
Sodium hydroxide (oven cleaner), baking soda, magnesium hydroxide (antacids), lime (calcium carbonate) for soils.
Antacid tablets neutralise excess stomach acid. Farmers spread lime to neutralise acidic soil.
No. Only bases that dissolve in water are alkalis. Copper oxide is a base that doesn't dissolve.

front: Why wear safety glasses with acids and alkalis?
back: Strong acids and alkalis are corrosive and can damage skin and eyes. Alkalis are especially dangerous to eyes.
